title: Indian Contract Act, 1872 — Section 14 (“Free consent” defined)

content.overview: Section 14 provides that consent is said to be free when it is not caused by — (1) coercion, as defined in section 15; (2) undue influence, as defined in section 16; (3) fraud, as defined in section 17; (4) misrepresentation, as defined in section 18; or (5) mistake, subject to sections 20, 21 and 22. Consent is said to be so caused when it would not have been given but for the existence of such coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation or mistake.
content.glance: Free consent = not caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation or mistake (ss. 15–18, 20–22).
content.study: Consent is free when not caused by coercion (s. 15), undue influence (s. 16), fraud (s. 17), misrepresentation (s. 18), or mistake (ss. 20–22). Consent is so caused when it would not have been given but for that factor. Free consent is an ingredient of a contract under s. 10; its absence yields voidability under ss. 19–19A (or voidness for bilateral mistake of fact under s. 20). Current-law framing: establish consent (s. 13); test each vitiating factor; apply the ‘but for’ causation test.

sections.heading: Five vitiating factors
sections.body: Coercion (s. 15); undue influence (s. 16); fraud (s. 17); misrepresentation (s. 18); mistake (ss. 20–22).

sections.heading: Causation
sections.body: Consent is so caused when it would not have been given but for the existence of such factor.

examples.title: Consent not free
examples.body: A’s consent is obtained by threat of an act forbidden by the IPC. Consent is not free under s. 14 read with s. 15.

hypotheticals.question: Does every hard bargain show absence of free consent?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Free consent is absent only when caused by one of the five statutory factors with ‘but for’ causation.

misconceptions.trap: Any pressure or bad bargain means consent is not free.
misconceptions.correction: Section 14 lists five specific causes; ordinary commercial pressure is not enough without one of those.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a Section 14 problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Establish consent (s. 13). II. Test coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation, mistake. III. Apply ‘but for’ causation. IV. Conclude on freeness and consequences (ss. 19–20).
